beats.say: Here is a formula with three letters: a equals b divided by c. We know a is 3 and b is 18, and we want a plus c.
We cannot add yet, because c is still hiding. So first, put the numbers we know into the formula.
3 equals 18 divided by c. So 18 has been split into equal parts, and each part is 3. How do we find c?

ask.ifNot: Ask how many 3s fit into 18. That is a division: 18 divided by 3.

beats.say: 18 divided by 3 is 6. So c is 6.
Careful: 6 is only c, not the answer. The question asks for a plus c.
a is 3 and c is 6. 3 plus 6 is 9.
Check c in the formula. 18 divided by 6 is 3, and a is 3. It fits.
So when a formula has a missing letter, put in what you know, find the missing one, and then answer what was really asked.
a equals b times c. We know a is 24 and c is one half. We need b minus a.
Put in what we know. 24 equals b times one half.
b times one half means half of b. So half of b is 24. What is b?

ask.ifNot: If half of b is 24, then b is two of those halves. 24 and 24 make 48. Halving 24 gives 12, but that goes the other way.

beats.say: Half of b is 24, so b is 24 times 2, which is 48.
Careful: the trap is to halve 24. But b times one half is 24, so b has to be bigger than 24, not smaller.
Now the question: b minus a. 48 minus 24 is 24.
Check b in the formula. 48 times one half is 24, and a is 24. It works.
Put in what you know, find the missing letter, and then do what the question asks with it.
L equals M times N. We know M is 13 and L is 78, and we must find N.
Put the numbers in place of their letters. 78 equals 13 times N.
13 times some number makes 78. What undoes times 13?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 13, we divide by 13.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 13. N is 78 divided by 13.
Count up in 13s. 13 times 5 is 65, and one more 13 makes 78. So 6 lots of 13 make 78.
So N is 6.
Careful not to add or multiply the 78 and the 13. N has to be small, because 13 times N is only 78.
Check: 13 times 6 is 78, and that matches L.
When a formula says one number times another, you find a missing one by dividing.
169 times 1 over x equals 13. First we find x. Then the question wants 3 x.
169 times 1 over x is the same as 169 divided by x. So 169 divided by x equals 13.
169 is split into x equal parts, and each part is 13. How do we find x?

ask.ifNot: Ask how many 13s fit into 169. That is 169 divided by 13.

beats.say: 13 times 10 is 130, and 13 times 3 is 39. 130 plus 39 is 169, so 13 lots of 13 make 169.
So x is 13.
Careful: x is not the answer yet. The question wants 3 x, which means 3 times x.
3 times 13 is 39.
Check x in the equation. 13 times 13 is 169, so 169 divided by 13 really is 13.
Find the letter first. Then read the question again to see what it really wants.

Check x in the equation. 25 times 25 is 625, so 625 divided by 25 really is 25.

Priya gives away one third of her ladoos, then one quarter of what is left, then eats 5, and 25 remain. We must find how many she made.

board.text: gave 1/3, then 1/4 of the rest, ate 5, left 25

beats.say: We know the end of the story, but not the start. So which way should we work?

ask.ifNot: We do not know the starting number, so we cannot go forwards. We do know the ending, 25, so we undo each step from there.

beats.say: Undo the last step first. She ate 5 and had 25 left, so before eating she had 25 plus 5, which is 30.
Before that, she gave her cousins one quarter of the ladoos she had left. So the 30 is the other 3 quarters.
If 3 quarters are 30, what is 1 quarter?

ask.ifNot: 3 equal parts make 30, so one part is 30 divided by 3. That is 10.

beats.say: One quarter is 10, so all 4 quarters are 40. She had 40 ladoos after the neighbours took their share.
Same idea again. The neighbours took one third, so the 40 is the other 2 thirds.
Half of 40 is 20, so one third is 20. And 3 thirds, the whole lot, is 60.
Priya made 60 ladoos.
Careful: the one quarter was a quarter of what was left, not of all 60. That is why we went one step at a time.
Check forwards. One third of 60 is 20, which leaves 40. One quarter of 40 is 10, which leaves 30.
And 30 take away the 5 she ate is 25. It matches the story.
When you know the end but not the start, work backwards and undo one step at a time.
Ravi has 600 rupees. He spends one quarter on books, gives 2 fifths of the rest to his sister, then spends one third of what is left on sweets. How much does he still have?
Start with the books. One quarter of 600 is 600 divided by 4, which is 150.
So 600 minus 150 leaves 450 rupees.
Next he gives 2 fifths to his sister. 2 fifths of which amount?

ask.ifNot: The question says from the remaining money. After the books, the remaining money is 450, so we take 2 fifths of 450.

beats.say: One fifth of 450 is 90, so 2 fifths is 180. His sister gets 180 rupees.
450 minus 180 leaves 270 rupees.
Last, the sweets. Again it is one third of what is left, so one third of 270. That is 90.
270 minus 90 leaves 180 rupees. That is what Ravi still has.
Careful: 180 turned up twice. The first 180 went to his sister. The 180 at the end is what Ravi keeps.
Check by adding it all back. 150 plus 180 plus 90 went out, which is 420. And 420 plus the 180 he kept is 600.
When a question says of the remaining money, find what is left after each step before you take the next fraction.
Arjun spends 2 fifths of his money on balls, then 3 quarters of the rest on a bat, and has 90 rupees left. We want the total he collected.

board.text: 2/5 on balls, 3/4 of rest on bat, ₹90 left

ask.ifNot: The whole is 4 quarters. Take away the 3 quarters spent on the bat, and 1 quarter is left.

beats.say: So the 90 rupees is one quarter of the money he had after the balls. All 4 quarters is 90 times 4, which is 360.
Now the balls. He spent 2 fifths of the total on them. So the 360 is how many fifths of the total?

ask.ifNot: The total is 5 fifths. 2 fifths went on balls, so 3 fifths were left, and that is the 360.

beats.say: 3 fifths is 360, so 1 fifth is 360 divided by 3, which is 120.
And the whole amount, 5 fifths, is 120 times 5. That is 600 rupees.
Careful: the 3 quarters came out of what was left after the balls, not out of the whole amount. That is why we undid the bat first.
Check forwards. 2 fifths of 600 is 240, which leaves 360. 3 quarters of 360 is 270, which leaves 90.
Know the end but not the start? Work backwards, one step at a time.
Sanya has two ribbons, 84 centimetres and 60 centimetres long. She cuts both into pieces of equal length, as long as possible, with no ribbon left over.

board.text: Ribbons: 84 cm and 60 cm. Longest equal pieces?

beats.say: Every piece is the same length, with nothing left over. So that length has to divide 84 and 60 exactly. Is that a factor of these numbers, or a multiple of them?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of these numbers is at least as big as the biggest of them, so it cannot divide them all exactly. A number that divides exactly is a factor.

beats.say: A factor of both, and we want the greatest one. So we need the highest common factor of 84 and 60.
The sure way is prime factors. Break each number down, smallest prime first. 84 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 7.
And 60 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.
Now look at the 7. It is a factor of 84, but not of 60. Does 7 go into the highest common factor?

choices: Yes, it is a prime factor
No, it must be in both lists
ask.ifNot: A common factor has to divide every number. 7 does not divide 60, so it stays out.

beats.say: So we mark only what both lists share: 2, 2 and 3. Every other prime is missing from at least one list.
Multiply them together. 2 times 2 times 3 is 12. So the highest common factor is 12.
So each piece is 12 centimetres long. That is our answer.
Check. 84 divided by 12 is 7, and 60 divided by 12 is 5. Nothing is left over.
And 7 and 5 have no common factor bigger than 1, so no bigger piece would fit both.
Longest equal pieces with nothing wasted means the highest common factor of the lengths.

board.text: Courtyard: 168 cm by 120 cm. Largest square tiles?

beats.say: Whole tiles must fit along each side of the floor, with no cutting. So the side of a tile has to divide 168 and 120 exactly. We want the greatest number that does. What is it called?

ask.ifNot: A common multiple is at least as big as the biggest of these numbers, so it could never divide them all. We need a factor of both numbers, and the greatest one: the highest common factor.

beats.say: So our job is to find the highest common factor of 168 and 120.
The sure way is prime factors. Break each number down, smallest prime first. 168 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 7.
And 120 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.
Now look at the 7. It is a factor of 168, but not of 120. Does 7 go into the highest common factor?

choices: Yes, it is a prime factor
No, it must be in both lists
ask.ifNot: A common factor has to divide every number. 7 does not divide 120, so it stays out.

beats.say: So we mark only what both lists share: 2, 2, 2 and 3. Every other prime is missing from at least one list.
Multiply them together. 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 is 24. So the highest common factor is 24.

Along the 168 side, 168 divided by 24 is 7 tiles. Along the 120 side, 120 divided by 24 is 5 tiles.
Careful: that is 5 rows of 7 tiles, so we multiply. Adding would only count two edges. 7 times 5 is 35.
So 35 tiles are needed.
Check. 7 tiles of 24 make 168, and 5 tiles of 24 make 120. The floor is covered exactly.
So the biggest square tile is the highest common factor of the two sides. Then count the tiles along each side and multiply.
